transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-03
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Sebastian (Redwood AE), Anika (Redwood SE), Jon (Redwood Solutions), Maya (CTO - Lyra), Ravi (Head of Platform), Elena (Security Architect), Tom (SRE)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance and fallbacks across Redwood Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments. Lyra needs multi-region failover, clear SLA / error budgets, KMS-based encryption, and deterministic fallback policies for model variants during outages. Next steps agreed: pricing + security docs, deep technical dive, benchmark run.

Topics covered:
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs for incident tolerance
- Multi-region routing and DNS/failover strategies
- Fallback policies: model variants, downgraded latency tiers, cache-first strategies
- SLA expectations, SLO/SLI discussion, error budgets and penalties
- Security: SOC2, KMS/HSM, audit logs, data residency and retention
- Operational runbooks, canary rollouts, tracing and debugging

Transcript:
[00:00] Sebastian: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, super excited to chat — quick intros?
[00:08] Maya: Hi I'm Maya, CTO at Lyra, we run the recommender and search infra, looking to add LLM features for product.
[00:12] Ravi: Ravi here, head of platform, primarily concerned with reliability and cost spikes.
[00:17] Tom: Tom SRE, will be the primary contact for the tests and benchmarks.
[00:22] Sebastian: Great, I'll hand over to Anika to go over architecture options and then we can deep dive into failover patterns.
[00:30] Anika: Cool. So at a high level Redwood offers hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Private (VPC / on-prem). From a reliability perspective hosted is fastest to get started, we have multi-region endpoints, automated fallback to compatible model variants, and a global routing layer. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and isolation. Private gives full control—you're basically running the runtime in your VPC or on-prem with our control plane.
[01:05] Ravi: When you say multi-region endpoints, is that active-active or active-passive? How's session affinity handled for KV cache?
[01:13] Anika: Good question. For hosted we support active-active across regions for stateless requests, but for stateful workloads with KV cache we recommend sticky routing. We do region-aware routing with a health-checking control plane; if a region degrades, traffic shifts to another region and we have transparent prefix/KV cache warming strategies. Sticky sessions can be configured at the route level.
[01:40] Tom: How do you warm caches? If we fail over, cold cache could kill latency.
[01:45] Anika: Right, so we have two levers: automated KV prefetch for common prefixes and replay-based warming during canary/failover. For Dedicated/Private you can export checkpoints or use our snapshot replication to seed caches in standby regions. It's not zero ms but it reduces p99 significantly.
[02:10] Maya: What's the SLA look like on hosted and dedicated? p99 latency? uptime?
[02:15] Sebastian: For hosted we publish region-level uptime commitments—we aim for 99.9% for paid tiers and have SLOs for p95/p99 latency per model class. Dedicated comes with contractual SLAs—99.95% availability and priority support, and we can define latency SLOs in the contract. Private is customer-managed so Redwood supports operational runbooks; we offer a managed support add-on with SLA.
[02:42] Elena: From security perspective: are requests encrypted end-to-end, and do you support our KMS? We need HSM-backed keys and audit logs retained for 1 year.
[02:51] Anika: Yes, TLS in transit, and encryption at rest. Dedicated and Private support customer KMS integration and HSM via standard interfaces; we can push logs to your SIEM or a secure S3 bucket. Audit logs retention is configurable—SOC2 whitepaper details and we can share data residency options.
[03:15] Ravi: Great. On fallback policies, we need deterministic behavior: if a high-capacity model is unavailable, we want automatic fallback to a smaller model but only up to a certain quality threshold, and we want to avoid cascading latency increases. How do you prevent those cascades?
[03:32] Anika: We recommend layered fallbacks: first try model variant fallback with a quality guardrail (we evaluate via eval sets and confidence heuristics), then a cached response path if prefix matches, then a degraded mode that returns structured/stubbed responses. We also have rate limiting and circuit breakers at the route level to protect downstream systems.
[03:55] Tom: Do you support synchronous vs asynchronous fallbacks? For some user flows we can accept async re-ranking later.
[04:00] Anika: Yep, you can choose sync fallback (smaller model) or return a cached placeholder and enqueue async re-score that updates the user later. This is configurable per route.
[04:12] Maya: For multi-region failover, how fast is traffic moved? We have strict p99 goals — if a region degrades how long before our app is impacted?
[04:20] Jon: Our healthchecks are aggressive for critical routes, typical failover is on the order of 10s to low 100s of seconds depending on DNS TTL and whether you're using our client with proactive connection draining. We also support BGP/Anycast patterns for lower cold start failovers on enterprise deployments. For Dedicated we can provision active-passive with warm standby nodes.
[04:45] Ravi: That 10s to 100s range is pretty wide. Can you guarantee something in the SLA for dedicated?
[04:52] Sebastian: For Dedicated we can commit to RTOs in the contract and have runbooks to orchestrate failovers; the actual numbers we'll map in SLOs—many customers set a 60s failover target for route-level healthchecks with warm standby.
[05:08] Elena: Also need full audit trail of failover events for compliance; we need to show sequence of events and operator actions.
[05:14] Anika: That's supported—every routing decision, healthcheck event and operator action is logged with timestamps and can be exported.
[05:24] Maya: How do you validate model quality post-fallback? We can't silently degrade user experience.
[05:29] Anika: We attach canary evals and quality monitors to rollouts. When fallback happens we record the request/response and run it against evaluation prompts; if quality dips below a configured threshold we can auto-roll back or notify. You can set alerts at the prompt-set or dataset level.
[05:50] Tom: On cost spikes — during incident-induced retries or retries from client side, is there a protection to avoid huge bill shocks?
[05:57] Sebastian: Yes, we have quota controls, per-route budget limits, and token caps. We also expose a cost-alerting API and circuit breakers to cut off or degrade service when you exceed thresholds. For Dedicated you can set burst capacity and bleed into hosted as a fallback if you want seamless failover with mixed-mode billing.
[06:18] Ravi: Mixed-mode sounds interesting — i.e. Dedicated primary, hosted overflow — but we need to know about data egress and compliance implications.
[06:25] Anika: Right, overflow to hosted is available but we'd treat customer data per your retention settings; you can opt-out of overflow or have encrypted payloads that only you can decrypt via KMS so hosted can't read plaintext. We'll document the exact flows in the security pack.
[06:42] Maya: For Private deployments, what's the operational burden? We have a small infra team.
[06:48] Jon: Private is heavier—you're responsible for the control plane components if you choose full air-gapped. Redwood offers a managed package where we run updates and healthchecks but it comes with an enterprise support contract. If you'd rather treat Private as last resort, Dedicated gives most of the isolation with less ops overhead.
[07:07] Tom: We also care about model version pinning and rollouts — if an update causes regressions, what's your rollback process?
[07:13] Anika: We have canary rollouts with automatic telemetry checks. If regressions detected we have automatic fallback to previous model version or route-level rollback. For Dedicated/Private you control the rollout schedule; Redwood provides tooling but you decide policies.
[07:29] Ravi: Can you share an example runbook for an incident?
[07:33] Anika: Yeah I can share a sanitized runbook; it includes detection, triage steps, circuit breaker flips, draining strategies, failover commands, and postmortem checklist. We'll attach it after the call.
[07:45] Maya: In terms of integrations, we use PagerDuty, Datadog, and Splunk — do you push alerts and traces?
[07:52] Jon: We integrate with PagerDuty for oncall routing, Datadog and Prometheus metrics ingestion, and you can forward logs to Splunk/S3. Tracing hooks exist for request-level traces; we can correlate tokens to traces with redaction rules.
[08:07] Elena: About encryption keys and separation of duty — we need an admin separation so Ops can't access customer keys. Is that supported?
[08:14] Anika: Yes, RBAC with least privilege, and key policies can be enforced so only certain principals or your KMS hold unescapeable keys. There's also audit logging for who accessed what.
[08:28] Tom: Two more practical questions: 1) during a regional outage if traffic routes to a smaller model we might see changed output that could harm UX — is there a way to label responses as degraded so product team can treat them differently? 2) Do you support client-side feature flags?
[08:40] Anika: 1) You can add response metadata flags (X-Redwood-Degraded: true) and include confidence scores. 2) We support SDK-level feature flags and you can wire them into your feature flagging service to switch routing policies on the fly.
[08:58] Sebastian: Okay quick recap — Lyra needs: multi-region active-active for stateless, sticky sessions for KV, deterministic layered fallback with quality gates, contract-level SLA for Dedicated with RTO guarantees, SOC2 + KMS/HSM support, audit trail for failovers, and benchmarks on traffic spikes. Action items we discussed earlier. Anything else?
[09:18] Maya: Procurement timeline — we're aiming to pick a vendor by end of Q1, want to run a pilot in January.
[09:25] Sebastian: That's doable; we'll prioritize the benchmark and security pack.
[09:29] Ravi: One ask — can we do a synthetic spike test that includes simulated region failure so we can validate failover and cache warming?
[09:36] Jon: Yes we can set that up; involve Tom's SREs and we'll coordinate.
[09:42] Tom: I'll send traffic traces and retention constraints after this call.
[09:46] Anika: We'll follow up with a proposed test plan and timeline.
[09:50] Maya: Cool, thanks everyone.
[09:52] Sebastian: Thanks all, we'll send materials and schedule the deep dive.
[09:58] -- end of transcript --
